intro: You've searched for a mortgage adviser near me, so you're likely looking for someone local who can help you understand your mortgage options and find a suitable deal. Whether you're buying your first home, remortgaging, or moving, a mortgage adviser can guide you through the process and recommend a mortgage that fits your circumstances.
need_heading: What people searching for a local mortgage adviser usually need
need_lead: Most people want clear, personalised advice from someone they can meet or speak to easily.
needs: You're a first-time buyer and want to know how much you can borrow and which mortgages you might qualify for.
You're remortgaging because your current deal is ending and you want to find a better rate or release equity.
You're self-employed or have irregular income and need an adviser who understands complex affordability.
You're moving home and need a mortgage that fits your new property and circumstances.
You want to understand the different types of mortgages and which one suits your long-term plans.
context: Mortgage advice in the UK is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Any adviser or broker you use should be authorised by the FCA, or be an appointed representative of an authorised firm, and you can check this on the FCA register. Advisers typically hold a qualification such as CeMAP.

Brokers must tell you whether they search the whole of the market or a limited panel of lenders, and how they are paid—whether by lender commission, a fee, or both. If something goes wrong, you can complain to the firm and then to the Financial Ombudsman Service.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when enquiring
tell: Your location and how far you're willing to travel to meet an adviser in person.
Whether you're buying your first home, moving, remortgaging, or exploring other reasons for mortgage advice.
Your employment status and how your income is earned, as this affects affordability and lender criteria.
The size of deposit or equity you have available, and the property price or value if relevant.
Any specific needs, such as advice on protection insurance or help for the self-employed.
Your preferred way of communicating—whether you want face-to-face meetings, phone calls, or online advice.
questions_heading: Questions to ask your mortgage adviser
questions: Are you authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, and what is your FCA registration number?
Do you search the whole of the market or a limited panel of lenders?
How are you paid—by lender commission, a fee from me, or both?
What qualifications do you hold, such as CeMAP?
Will you also discuss protection insurance, such as life cover or income protection, as part of your advice?
What is your process for keeping me informed and how often will you update me?

faqs.q: How do I check that a mortgage adviser is properly authorised?
faqs.a: You can check the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) register to see if an adviser or broker is authorised or an appointed representative of an authorised firm. It's a good idea to do this before you share any personal or financial information.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a mortgage adviser and a mortgage broker?
faqs.a: The terms are often used interchangeably. A mortgage adviser recommends suitable mortgages based on your circumstances, while a broker may search the market and handle the application. Both should be authorised by the FCA.

faqs.q: Will a mortgage adviser charge me a fee?
faqs.a: Advisers and brokers must tell you how they are paid—whether by lender commission, a fee from you, or both. You should ask for this in writing before you proceed so you understand any costs involved.

faqs.q: Can a mortgage adviser help if I'm self-employed?
faqs.a: Yes, many advisers have experience with self-employed applicants and can help you prepare evidence of income and find lenders that accept your circumstances. It's worth mentioning your employment status when you enquire.

extra_heading: Choosing someone you can actually get to
extra: Searching for a mortgage adviser near me suggests location matters to you, perhaps because you would rather sit down face to face than deal with everything by phone or email. That is a reasonable instinct, especially if you want to go through documents together or ask questions as they occur to you. It is worth thinking early about how far you are genuinely willing to travel, since a slightly longer journey may open up an adviser whose specialism matches your situation.

Distance is only one part of the decision. When you contact an adviser, ask how they usually work with clients: whether the first appointment is in their office, at your home, or by phone or video, and who you will actually deal with day to day. Some firms operate locally but handle most of the process remotely, which may suit you better than it first seems. It also helps to ask how quickly they tend to respond and how they keep you updated while an application is under way.

Before you settle on anyone, check that the firm is authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, or is an appointed representative of an authorised firm, using the FCA register. Ask whether they search the whole of the market or a limited panel of lenders, and get their charges explained in writing so you can weigh up what each local option offers. iComply introduces you to a UK mortgage broker who quotes you directly, so you can compare for yourself.

extra_faqs.q: Does a mortgage adviser near me have to meet me in person?
extra_faqs.a: No. Many advisers work by phone or video as well as face to face, and some handle the whole process remotely. It is worth asking how they prefer to work before you decide whether travelling to see them is necessary.

extra_faqs.q: Is a local mortgage adviser better than one further away?
extra_faqs.a: Not necessarily. Being close by can make meetings easier, but what matters most is that the adviser understands your circumstances and that you are comfortable with how they work. Compare how each one searches the market, how they are paid, and how they communicate.

extra_faqs.q: What should I have ready for a first meeting with a local adviser?
extra_faqs.a: It helps to bring proof of identity and address, details of your income and employment, and information about any deposit, savings or existing mortgage. Having these to hand means the adviser can give you a clearer picture of what may be available to you.
